view: The ruined garden pictures ostentatious charity or apparently good works done for display: worldly benefit or praise may accrue, but their reward vanishes when needed at Judgment.
note: Some notes specify the worldly benefit and others the lost reward or impossibility of repentance.

view: The garden pictures charity ruined by later reminders, reproach, injury, or abuse of its recipient; the spoiled deed cannot be restored when its reward is needed.
note: This contextual application differs from the view that the image specifically repeats ostentatious spending.

view: The garden parable continues the preceding warning against nullifying charity through reminders and harm, rather than beginning an unrelated subject.
note: Al-Ṭabarī favors the contextual link; Ibn ʿAṭiyya favors it over a second specific parable for ostentation.

view: The garden is a counterpart to the earlier soil-covered stone stripped bare by rain, another picture of lost charitable reward.
Following the favorable images of sincere spending, this final garden image presents their disastrous opposite: hope nears harvest, then showy or injurious giving ruins it.
The image also broadly covers any hypocrite or unbeliever who thinks he has good deeds but finds nothing when they are needed; its wording can apply beyond one form of invalidated charity.
note: Ibn ʿAṭiyya rejects restricting it to a second specific ostentation example; al-Ṭabrisī says the three reported applications fit.

view: A person begins with obedience or good deeds but later follows Satan into sins, or ends life in corruption, destroying the earlier work when it is most needed.
note: Reports vary between a final evil act, persistent late sin, and a wealthy worshipper tempted by Satan; ʿUmar accepts Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation.

view: A sharper version says late shirk or a major sin can void faith, charity, and other earlier good work, with the person dying an unbeliever.
The image depicts a person who neglects obedience while occupied with worldly pleasure or error until death, after which all becomes regret and the lost opportunity cannot be recovered.
note: This differs from the account of good deeds later destroyed by sin.

view: The disbeliever's deeds or temporary livelihood fail at resurrection: unlike the believer's stored honor, the disbeliever finds no good, cannot return to make amends, and faces lasting punishment.
note: Some reports add that pride and doubt of meeting God incur the punishment.

view: The image applies to an owner given youth and wealth who fails to act before both are taken away.
The garden symbolizes a person's deeds in general, without specifying what corrupts them.
The fruitful garden represents what a person fashioned or achieved in youth; one report depicts a man wasting it then being unable to rebuild it in old age.
Faith and good deeds resemble gardens whose reward can be destroyed by disbelief, ostentation, reproach, injury, or other corrupt motives at Judgment.
note: Al-Rāzī and al-Zamakhsharī include outwardly good acts done without seeking God's pleasure.

view: The Islamic polity is also a garden preparing eternal blessing; coercive unbelieving injustice, immorality, and lost resolve can devastate this life and the afterlife.
The image also depicts a seeker who rises toward the divine or unseen realm but turns back to worldly illusion, wasting the effort.
A good deed done for God's pleasure is a garden; later ego motions conflict like a whirlwind that Satan exploits through whispering.
Self-regard or ostentation is the fire that consumes a deed at the very time its reward is needed.
Sincere giving receives replacement and honor, while hypocritical spending wastes wealth and reward; faithful deeds are a flourishing crop and failed deeds a ruined bargain.
Works bear fruit through sincerity at their root, so worshippers should inspect intention before and during worship and resist ostentatious thoughts.
Ostentation grows from love of this world and immediate pleasure; remove its roots and cultivate the opposite disposition.
Ostentation enters when one expects to be noticed, desires praise and rank, then accepts that desire; each stage should be rejected.
A prayer attributed to the Prophet asks that his broadest provision come in old age near life's end.
Muʿādh reports that the Prophet, sending him to Yemen, advised sincere religion, for which a little work suffices.
ʿAlī asks forgiveness for devotional acts whose intentions his heart later contradicted.
ʿUmar asked the Companions what the garden parable meant and pressed them to say whether they knew; Ibn ʿAbbās then explained and ʿUmar accepted his answer.
note: Some versions say the Companions were silent or deferred to God and His Messenger.

view: The report of Ibn ʿAbbās interpreting the rich worshipper's deeds as ruined by later sins is transmitted by al-Bukhārī; Ibn Kathīr notes it was reported by al-Bukhārī alone, while another note lists additional transmitters.
note: The notes give differing transmission descriptions without resolving them.

view: Ibn ʿAbbās's reading of good work ruined by late sin is preferred over restricting the parable to reproach or ostentation because of his standing and ʿUmar's acceptance.
The old garden owner is the picture of ruin at the moment of greatest need: he lacks strength to earn or replant, and his weak dependents cannot restore the lost livelihood.
note: The analogy is to deeds lost at death or Judgment; some notes emphasize that repentance is then impossible.

view: Old age heightens need and regret while reducing the ability to earn, rebuild, or enjoy earlier effort.
note: Al-Māwardī adds that old age can make one forget youthful effort and weaken hope.

view: Weak young children or needy dependents cannot earn or help the aged owner, intensifying his reliance on the garden; an elder with strong children would have another recourse.
An aged parent is especially tender and protective toward weak children, making the loss more painful.
The weak offspring are part of the parable's stated image.
Janna means a densely planted, shading orchard or its tree growth; it may refer to the trees themselves or to land containing them.
note: When taken as land, trees are understood for rivers to run beneath; al-Ālūsī favors the tree-growth sense.

view: Al-Ḥasan reads the garden in the plural as جنات.
A report says every kind of earthly tree, even colocynth, exists in Paradise.
Palms and grapevines are singled out as the finest, most valued and useful garden trees, while the garden has other fruit too.
note: Some notes specify abundance or attractiveness as well as superiority.

view: The Qur'an names the palm tree itself but grapes by their fruit because the entire palm is useful, while a vine's main benefit is its fruit.
Nakhīl is a collective noun or a plural of the collective nakhl; the date palm name may be masculine or feminine.
One derivation connects nakhīl to sifting or selection; the palm is noted as noble, broadly useful, and distinctive in pollination and growth.
ʿInab is a collective for grapes, ʿinaba its unit, and aʿnāb its plural; ʿinbāʾ is another extended feminine form that does not decline.
Min explains the garden's type or predominant crop without excluding other plants; the phrase can serve as a nominative adjective of the garden.
The running-rivers clause can modify the garden or, by pronoun reference, the palms; it can also be a circumstantial clause, or a predicate of تكون.
The rivers run below the garden's trees, not beneath the earth itself.
An hār names broad channels carrying flowing water, one of an orchard's best features.

Running rivers suggest fertile land and recall other images of water below gardens, including Paradise; this irrigated garden contrasts with the preceding rain-fed ridge orchard, whose water failure would cost less.
The garden has every kind of fruit beyond its dates and grapes, heightening the loss when it burns.
Every fruit can mean a great variety or abundance, not literal possession of each fruit.
Fruits may mean all the benefits or yield of the garden, as with the two gardens in al-Kahf.
note: Al-Ālūsī discusses but does not prefer this sense.

view: In the clause, له is a fronted predicate and the من phrase appears to occupy the subject position, requiring an analysis of its underlying noun.
An omitted noun such as provision, fruit, or food is understood before the min phrase, which describes it; poetic and Qur'anic parallels support this solution.
Al-Akhfash treats min as extra, yielding 'he has all fruits,' where all can mean abundance rather than literal totality.
note: Unlike Kufan and Basran restrictions, al-Akhfash imposes no condition on extra min.

view: Extra min is rejected under Kufan or standard Basran rules, and because literal possession of every fruit is implausible; Abū al-Baqāʾ allows it if abundance is intended.
note: This disputes al-Akhfash's extra-min analysis.

view: The wāw introduces a circumstantial clause about the owner, with an implied قد in some analyses; the weak-offspring clause is also circumstantial.
note: The circumstantial analysis competes with coordination by meaning and the implied-law explanation.

view: The past verb after a future wish is licensed because wadd may take either أن or an implied لو; Arabic can use the conditional pattern of one for the other, with past wording bearing future sense.
note: Poetry and other verses are cited as parallels; Abū Ḥayyān objects to treating old age as part of the wish, while al-Ālūsī resists that objection.

view: Another analysis coordinates by the sense of the wish: would one wish to have a garden and then be struck by old age?
note: Abū al-Baqāʾ calls this semantically weak; al-Zamakhsharī favors it.

view: Semantic coordination is criticized because old age itself is not wished for and because it changes the wording unnecessarily; a reply says the rejected object is the combined state of garden ownership and old age.
The storm clause can coordinate with the earlier adjectival description of the garden, beginning with 'of palms' and continuing through what follows.
Wudd means love or wishing, with some describing it as complete love; 'would one of you love?' addresses each person.
The opening question repudiates or denies the prospect of such a calamity, stressing how intensely one would wish to avoid it.
note: Bursevī distinguishes rejecting this future wish from denying an act already happening.

view: A report says ʿUmar read yuḥibbu, 'would love,' in the opening question.
Aḥad here means any one of you distributively and does not require a negative construction.
Saying old age 'struck him' gives the event a stronger force than merely saying he grew old; repeated 'struck' marks the impact of each calamity.
Kibar means old age; kabīr can describe size or age even for one thing, whereas kathīr necessarily denotes number.
Weak can describe young, dependent, or poor people; poetry and another verse illustrate the needy sense.
Ḍuʿafāʾ and ḍiʿāf are regular plurals of ḍaʿīf, reflecting the two plural patterns of فعيل.
A variant reads the weak offspring as ḍiʿāf rather than ḍuʿafāʾ.
Iʿṣār is a violent rotating wind or dust column rising from the ground toward the sky, also called zawbaʿa; its plural is aʿāṣīr.
note: Al-Ālūsī adds that colliding air currents may make it descend or rise and uproot trees or snatch boats.

view: Some identify iʿṣār especially with a lethal scorching wind or samūm, rather than defining it only by its rotating shape.
Other reports gloss the whirlwind simply as wind or violent wind.
Poetic lines by an unnamed poet, al-Kumayt, and Yazīd al-Ḥimyarī, along with a whirlwind proverb, are cited as Arabic evidence for iʿṣār or its plural.
note: The proverb says that one who is a wind has met a stronger whirlwind.

view: The wind-name may derive from its twisting like wrung cloth; Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls this weak, while al-Qurṭubī endorses it as matching the visible coiling column.
Another proposed derivation links iʿṣār to winds squeezing clouds or contents; muʿṣirāt can mean rain-laden or compressed clouds, and some take it as winds.
Al-Jawharī also calls a whirlwind zawbaʿa or umm zawbaʿa; the name can also denote a chief of the jinn.
The whirlwind's fire is intense scorching samūm, a hot wind that burns what it strikes.
note: Al-Suddī distinguishes the wind itself from the samūm within it; Ibn ʿĀshūr treats fire as an emphatic likeness.

view: A competing account says the destructive whirlwind contains severe cold, frost, or hail, which can burn and ruin the garden.
note: This differs from the scorching-samūm explanation.

view: The whirlwind's destructive heat or cold may be a breath of Hell, as suggested by a Prophetic report about intense heat and the Fire's complaint.
note: Ibn ʿAṭiyya also leaves literal fire possible.

view: A report says the samūm from which jinn were created is one seventieth of the Fire; one explanation identifies that as the afterlife's Fire.
note: The notes attribute the saying to Ibn ʿAbbās or Ibn Masʿūd.

view: One alternative takes the fire in the whirlwind as lightning.
Naming a fire-bearing whirlwind and leaving fire indefinite magnifies the terror of the destructive event.

The masculine pronoun in فيه agrees with the masculine إعصار; نار can be the subject of the prepositional phrase as predicate, or the phrase can modify إعصار, with the latter nearer simple-adjective parse preferred.
The garden itself burned: the fiery wind consumed its fruit and trees, leaving the aged owner without their livelihood.
The successive fāʾ marks the storm striking after the orchard has ripened and become useful, heightening the disaster just as harvest approaches.
Iḥtaraqat is the intransitive or inchoative effect of causative aḥraqa: the garden was burned and burned up.
Arabic ḥaraqa nāb can describe a man's intensified anger or tooth grinding; the cited line allows nominative or accusative nāb and transitive or intransitive usage.
The earlier garden image is damaged from below at the roots, while this one is struck from above at the branches, showing two directions from which harm may arrive.
'Thus' points to the just-mentioned parables or signs.
God clarifies signs by proofs or parables so people can understand religious truths, heed consequences, and act.
note: Ibn ʿĀshūr stresses that tangible pictures bring abstract truths near; Elmalılı adds applying principles to circumstances.

view: The clarified signs also encompass earlier spending, striving, Abraham, and ruined-town examples, establishing oneness, messengership, reward, punishment, or religion's truth.
The call to reflect asks people to obey after understanding the parable.
People should ponder God's parables and take their lesson; only the learned truly grasp them, as 29:43 states.
Reflection should turn thought from the passing world to the arriving, enduring afterlife, encouraging deeds for it.
Reflection can lead one to recognize God's majesty and lordship and cease taking other protectors.
Because لعل expresses hope, one explanation treats it as hope from a human perspective; a Muʿtazilite argument instead takes it as evidence that God intended all people to believe.
note: The interpretations differ over what divine use of a hope particle implies.

view: Thought arranges known matters to discover unknown ones; one maxim says action's end begins reflection and reflection's end begins action.
Worship needs reflection about both the beginning and end of action, as a builder prepares a project and its consequences.

The connected spending passage appears to have been revealed as a unit, moving from multiplied reward and sincere giving through invalidated charity, sound wealth, needy recipients, and promised reward.
The spending passage orders its teaching by purpose, manner, quality of wealth, recipient, and reward.
The discussion next turns to where, how, and to whom obligatory and voluntary spending should be given.
The passage employs transitions between particular and general statements, allusion, simile, ellipsis, specification, parable, and metaphor.
The date and grape detail fills out what the earlier garden parable left general; the orchard's screened inner space makes the desired garden vivid.
Al-Aʿshā's poem heightens the old owner's anticipation of the garden's yield and dependence on it, sharpening the sense of impending loss.
The wholly useful palm resembles a believer beneficial in every part; the vine's branching in all directions resembles piety that brings honor in every direction.
The word taḥūt is used of people low beneath others' feet and unnoticed.
Arabic may combine different grammatical forms with overlapping meanings, such as mā with in or allāʾ with alladhīna, but the same repetition of identical forms is not licensed.
Abū's reading of 'the unbelievers wish' uses a subjunctive verb after law in the sense of an, whereas an indicative would follow law directly.
Just as the elderly owner cannot rebuild the garden or his children's lost livelihood, a person whose work ends at death cannot then repent or repair it.
Love of wealth and status, pride, conceit, and miserliness can corrupt charity and block discernment; contemplation would expose the harm.
